```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  message = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE,
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
```

A trip (voyage) is the part of a vessel track between leaving port and
returning to port. In ramb, getting from raw pings to trips is the
entry of the fishing-activity flow: flag the pings (step 0), then cut
the track into voyages and put the trip back on each ping (step 1).

We use the `dansk` example data (Danish VMS pings) and the
`dansk_harbours` polygons, both shipped with the package. First, rename
to the grammar column names so every function runs on its defaults —
alternatively, pass e.g. `vid = vessel_id, time = time_stamp` to each
call.

```{r}
library(ramb)
library(dplyr)

d <-
  dansk |>
  arrange(vessel_id, time_stamp) |>
  rename(vid = vessel_id, time = time_stamp)
```

## Step 0: flag the pings

Flagging sets a `ping_flag` column; no row is ever dropped. A position
that is a placeholder rather than a fix is `"invalid"`:

```{r}
d <- d |> rb_flag_ping_invalid()
```

A position the vessel cannot have reached — implied speed above
`kn_max` knots — is flagged. Five `method`s differ in how much of the
surrounding track they consult; `"clean"` is the fast default:

```{r}
d <- d |> rb_flag_ping_impossible(method = "clean")
d |> count(ping_flag)
```

A third flagger, `rb_flag_ping_duplicate()`, marks the lower-priority
feed's copy when several feeds report the same fix.

Finally, tag each ping with the port polygon it lies in. `port_id` is a
value in port, `NA` at sea — this is the column trips are cut on. The
flagged pings are set aside (kept in `flagged` for the maps below);
nothing is deleted:

```{r}
harbours <- dansk_harbours |> rename(port_id = SI_HARB)

flagged <- d |> filter(!is.na(ping_flag))

d <-
  d |>
  filter(is.na(ping_flag)) |>
  rb_flag_ping_port(harbours)
```

## Step 1: cut the track into voyages

`rb_cut_trip_voyages()` offers three rules (`method`); here we compare
two of them:

* `method = "runs"`: every run of pings in port, however short, ends a
  voyage.
* `method = "jepol"`: the ICES VMS datacall rule (`define_trips_pol`).
  A voyage runs from the first ping at sea to the first ping back in
  port; voyages shorter than `min_dur_h` hours are dropped, and voyages
  longer than `max_dur_h` hours are split at long gaps between pings.

```{r}
jepol <- rb_cut_trip_voyages(d, method = "jepol")
runs  <- rb_cut_trip_voyages(d, method = "runs")
```

Both return one row per voyage: vessel, year, voyage id, start and end
time, the ports departed from and returned to, and the number of pings.

```{r}
jepol
```

The two rules largely agree on these data; the jepol rule drops a few
short harbour-to-harbour runs:

```{r}
count(jepol, vid, name = "voyages_jepol") |>
  full_join(count(runs, vid, name = "voyages_runs"), by = "vid")
```

A third rule, `method = "stays"`, cuts the track at port *stays* found
by `rb_find_trip_stays()` — stays being longer stops, so brief harbour
passages do not end a voyage. That is the rule used in the full
fishing-activity flow.

## Putting the trip back on the pings

`rb_assign_trip()` joins the voyage table back onto the pings. Each
ping gets a `trip_id` and a `trip_basis` — `"reconstructed"` when the
trip was rebuilt from the track, `"none"` where no voyage covers the
ping (the port pings here):

```{r}
p <- d |> rb_assign_trip(jepol)
p |> count(trip_basis)
```

## The cut, in maps

Toggle the layers (top right of each map) to look at one trip at a
time.

### Two clean trips

`EX_3`, September 2020 — two voyages out of port 917, no flagged pings
anywhere in their windows:

* **Voyage 3** (Sep 15, ~8 h at sea): a simple out-and-back day trip,
  south along the coast and home again.
* **Voyage 4** (Sep 17–18, ~12 h): an overnight trip — out in the
  evening, fishing through the night, back before dawn.

```{r}
library(mapview)

as_line <- function(x) {
  x |>
    arrange(time) |>
    sf::st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326) |>
    sf::st_combine() |>
    sf::st_cast("LINESTRING") |>
    sf::st_sf()
}

ex3 <- p |> filter(vid == "EX_3", lubridate::year(time) == 2020, voyage_id %in% 3:4)

mapview(harbours |> filter(port_id == 917),
        col.regions = "orange", alpha.regions = 0.4, layer.name = "Port 917") +
  mapview(ex3 |> filter(voyage_id == 3) |> as_line(),
          color = "steelblue", lwd = 2, layer.name = "Voyage 3 (Sep 15)") +
  mapview(ex3 |> filter(voyage_id == 4) |> as_line(),
          color = "darkred", lwd = 2, layer.name = "Voyage 4 (Sep 17-18)")
```

On clean tracks like these the choice of cutting rule is immaterial:
each run at sea is one voyage under both `"runs"` and `"jepol"`, and
the two tables row-match exactly. The rules only earn their keep when
the track is less tidy — as next.

### When the rules disagree

`EX_10`, July 2014, out of port 141. The runs rule cuts seven voyages
this year, the jepol rule five — the difference is one afternoon:

* **The day's trip** (blue): out at 04:08, back at 11:25. Both rules
  agree on it.
* **Two mini-voyages** (red): brief out-and-backs the same afternoon,
  at 14:37 and 14:53, each under ten minutes. `"runs"` takes every port
  departure literally and makes them voyages 5 and 6; `"jepol"` drops
  any voyage shorter than `min_dur_h` (0.5 h), so these pings end up
  with `trip_basis = "none"`.
* **One flagged ping** (black): a `"forward"` flag from step 0, set
  aside before cutting, so it takes no part in either rule.

```{r}
ex10 <-
  d |>
  rb_assign_trip(runs) |>
  filter(vid == "EX_10", lubridate::date(time) == as.Date("2014-07-18"))

mapview(harbours |> filter(port_id == 141),
        col.regions = "orange", alpha.regions = 0.4, layer.name = "Port 141") +
  mapview(ex10 |> filter(voyage_id == 4) |> as_line(),
          color = "steelblue", lwd = 2, layer.name = "Day trip (04:08-11:25)") +
  mapview(ex10 |> filter(voyage_id %in% 5:6) |>
            sf::st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326),
          col.regions = "red", cex = 4, layer.name = "Mini-voyages (runs only)") +
  mapview(flagged |> filter(vid == "EX_10", lubridate::date(time) == as.Date("2014-07-18")) |>
            sf::st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326),
          col.regions = "black", cex = 6, layer.name = "Flagged ping")
```

Which is right? If the afternoon runs were the skipper moving berth or
testing the engine, dropping them (jepol) is honest; if gear was in the
water, only `"runs"` keeps them. The third rule, `"stays"`, goes the
other way entirely: it ends a voyage only at a *stay*, so a brief
harbour passage mid-trip would not split the day's trip either.

### Trouble pings inside a voyage

The next day on the same vessel. Voyage 5 (Jul 19, 04:12–12:30) sails
with eight flagged pings in its window:

* **The voyage** (blue): the track as kept after step 0.
* **The flagged pings** (red): a `"vmask"` flag near port in the
  morning, then a burst of seven `"forward"` flags in the last quarter
  of an hour before landing — the classic signature of a GPS glitch
  burst on the final approach.

```{r}
v5 <- p |> filter(vid == "EX_10", voyage_id == 5, lubridate::year(time) == 2014)
f5 <- flagged |>
  filter(vid == "EX_10", lubridate::date(time) == as.Date("2014-07-19"))

mapview(harbours |> filter(port_id == 141),
        col.regions = "orange", alpha.regions = 0.4, layer.name = "Port 141") +
  mapview(v5 |> as_line(),
          color = "steelblue", lwd = 2, layer.name = "Voyage 5 (Jul 19)") +
  mapview(f5 |> sf::st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326),
          col.regions = "red", cex = 6, layer.name = "Flagged pings")
```

Because the flags are set aside first, neither cutting rule is confused
by the glitch: the voyage is cut on the clean pings, and the voyage
window then covers the gap. This is why step 0 flags rather than drops
— the flagged pings still exist for audit, but they cannot bend the
trip boundaries.

From here the flow continues with the logbook record (step 2): which
declared trip or haul covers each ping. `rb_link_trip_logbook()` builds
the VMS-to-logbook crosswalk for that.
